newsitem.title: USA: Most IMM currencies end higher, but off peaks.
newsitem.headline: Most IMM currencies end higher, but off peaks.

text.p: Most IMM currency futures ended higher, but fell from session peaks late on speculation that U.S. Treasury secretary Robert Rubin will announce overnight the U.S.'s commitment for a higher U.S. dollar, analysts said.
"Someone is placing a large bet that Rubin will make a statement overnight," George Tzanetatos, vice president at Merrill Lynch, said.

The U.S. administration did not respond during U.S. daytime hours to reports quoting Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara. Sakakibara's comments that the dollar/yen upward correction was over rattled U.S. traders all day.
"I think it's baloney," one floor trader said about Sakakibara's comments. "It's just noise in an otherwise bullish dollar/yen trend."
December yen remained near the upper end of its daily range at $0.009033, or about 111.30 spot yen, and failed to rise to resistance at $0.009053 or 111.00 spot.

"I think the best you can say is that the dollar/yen is trading in a lower trading range," Michael Malpeded, senior currency analyst at Refco, Inc, said. "Japan's economic numbers don't justify higher interest rates, and we haven't seen how the U.S. feels about Sakakibara's comments."
Projections from Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers, that Rubin is likely to de-emphasize the importance of a strong dollar did not weaken the U.S. dollar.
In fact, Jasinowski's comments have raised the likelihood that Rubin will deliver a much stronger statement supporting a higher U.S. dollar, analysts said.
"The more there is on the table, the more forceful Rubin's comments will be," Tzanetatos siad.
He said U.S. corporates were heavy buyers in the afternoon, sending December yen to $0.008945, or 112.30 spot.

One firm was active in the yen futures pit, buying about 1,500 at $0.009008 and selling 2,500 at the $0.008989 level, one floor trader said. He said the yen's volatility changed the direction in cash cross rates and weighed on currencies.

Likewise, December marks fell to $0.6620, as the U.S. dollar rose to about 1.5175 spot marks, and December Swiss francs weakened to $0.7870, as the U.S. dollar rose through 1.2735 spot in the afternoon.
"There are very substantial orders going through," Tzanetatos said about corporate demand for dollars. "Fifty million dollars, $100 million went through like nothing."

Canadian dollars managed to set a contract high at $0.7545 as the U.S. dollar rallied. Talk circulated on the floor that the Bank of Canada might cut rates after the release of Friday's employment data, traders said.
Mexican pesos trimmed losses briefly in reaction to Mexico's 1997 budget proposal, but December still clung to declines.

At the end of pit trade, December yen was up $0.000136 at $0.008958, marks rose $0.0018 at $0.6625, Swiss francs were $0.0018 higher at $0.7877, sterling was up $0.0060 at $1.6466, and Can dollars were off $0.0003 at $0.7536.
